posts.title: Mingfeng Jiang shows that ignoring death after spawning distorts squid stock assessments
posts.summary: A new length–age structured model treats post-spawning death as part of squid population dynamics, and shows what goes wrong when assessments leave it out.
body: OFEL PhD student Mingfeng Jiang has developed a stock assessment model for squid and other semelparous species, animals that spawn once and die soon afterwards. The model builds death after spawning directly into the population dynamics, giving a more faithful picture of how these populations change over time. The study is published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.

Most stock assessment models were designed for fish that spawn many times over their lives. Squid follow a different life history: an individual reproduces once and then dies. When models built for repeat-spawning fish are applied to squid, they can misrepresent population dynamics and give a misleading view of stock status.

To address this, the team added post-spawning mortality as an explicit process in a length–age structured assessment model, so that the model follows the life history of semelparous species. They then measured how much assessment results change when this process is ignored.

The work extends integrated length–age assessment methods to semelparous species and strengthens the toolkit for studying cephalopod population dynamics. More accurate assessments give a firmer scientific basis for conserving cephalopod stocks and managing squid fisheries sustainably around the world.

Mingfeng Jiang and postdoctoral researcher Sisong Dong are co-first authors. Professor Fan Zhang and Professor Xinjun Chen are co-corresponding authors. The study was carried out with Professor André E. Punt's team at the University of Washington.

paper.title: Ignoring death after spawning misrepresents the population dynamics of marine semelparous species
